captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 9. In this lesson: Whose story is it?
Compare first-person and third-person narration and their effects.
Here are some new words. Narrator. The person or voice that tells a story. First person.
A story told by ‘I’, a character inside the story. Third person. A story told using ‘he’, ‘she’ or ‘they’.
And some more words. Omniscient. Knowing everything, including all characters' thoughts. Perspective.
The point of view from which something is seen. Intimate. Very close and personal.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: the person or voice that tells a story?
Now some grammar: Narrative tenses. Use the past simple for main events,
the past continuous for background actions, and the past perfect for events that happened earlier.
For example: It was raining when I arrived. For example: She had already left by the time he called.
Now listen, and read along. Two versions of one moment. Version A, first person.
I knew I shouldn't have opened the box.
My hands were shaking as I lifted the lid, and for a second I couldn't breathe.
Inside, wrapped in old newspaper, was the watch my father had lost the year before he died.
I had searched for it everywhere. How had it got here? Version B, third person, omniscient.
Lena lifted the lid slowly, her hands shaking. Inside lay the watch her father had lost years before.
She did not know that her brother, Marek,
was watching from the doorway – or that he had hidden the watch there himself, six months earlier,
unable to explain why he had taken it.
Another question. The video will stop. Who is the narrator in Version A?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like narrator, first person, third person.
You practised narrative tenses. And you read Two versions of one moment. Now try the practice questions.
See you next time!

captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 9. In this lesson: Can we trust her?
Recognise an unreliable narrator and use reported speech with tense changes.
Here are some new words. Unreliable. Not able to be trusted. Reliable. Able to be trusted. Contradict.
Say the opposite of what someone else has said.
And some more words. Claim. Say that something is true without proof. Insist.
Say something firmly, again and again. Evidence. Facts that show something is true.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: not able to be trusted?
Now some grammar: Reported speech. In reported speech,
tenses usually move one step back: present becomes past, past becomes past perfect, will becomes would,
can becomes could. For example: ‘I am innocent.’ becomes She said she was innocent.
For example: ‘I didn't take it.’ becomes He said he hadn't taken it.
For example: ‘I will help.’ becomes She said she would help.
Now listen, and read along. The missing cake. Let me be clear: I did not eat the cake.
I want that on the record. Mum left it on the kitchen table at four o'clock.
I was in my room, reading quietly, the whole afternoon. Well – almost the whole afternoon.
I did go downstairs once, but only for a glass of water. When Mum came home, the cake was gone.
My sister said she had seen me in the kitchen. She is always making things up.
I told Mum that I had been upstairs the entire time, which is basically true.
Mum asked why there was chocolate on my sleeve. I said that I had no idea.
Honestly, chocolate gets everywhere in this house. Anyway, I insist that I am innocent.
And I'm not even hungry tonight. Not even slightly.
Another question. The video will stop. What does the narrator claim?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like unreliable, reliable, contradict. You practised reported speech.
And you read The missing cake. Now try the practice questions. See you next time!
